item.title: Numerical Modeling for Fusion Energy
item.description:
This work focuses on the computational challenges of modeling how electrically conducting fluids behave under strong magnetic fields, a key problem in fusion reactor design. These flows are complex and turbulent, making it difficult and costly to predict how heat moves through them using traditional 3D simulations.

To address this, the study introduces a stable simulation method (a 3 scale-variational multiscale finite element method) that captures the essential flow behavior without the heavy computational cost. By simplifying the problem while maintaining accuracy, the approach provides a practical path toward faster, more reliable modeling of liquid-metal cooling systems in fusion and other high-energy applications.

Lighting a Miniature Sun on Earth

With the growing demand for clean and sustainable energy, the world has made significant strides in renewable sources such as wind, solar, and hydro. But there’s another technology—still experimental—that promises to deliver clean, continuous power on a scale no existing renewable can match.

That technology is nuclear fusion.

To picture it, imagine standing beside a machine designed to recreate the power of the Sun, not in space, but right here on Earth. This ambitious effort is taking shape in southern France, inside a massive structure known as ITER. It’s a collaboration of 35 nations, all working together to unlock clean, virtually limitless energy through fusion.

One of the biggest challenges in a fusion reactor is preventing it from melting itself. To keep the system cool, engineers must circulate a coolant through a structure called the blanket, a network of channels that sits just inches away from plasma burning hotter than the core of the Sun.

Several reactor designs have been proposed, using different coolants such as water, helium, liquid metals (like lithium or lead–lithium alloys), and molten salts (such as Flibe or Flinabe). Each option brings its own balance of safety, efficiency, and engineering complexity.

In some designs, liquid metals are preferred over molten salts for their superior heat transfer and thermal conductivity, enabled by their high boiling points. They are also considered safer and more stable than water under the extreme conditions of a fusion environment {%cite tillack2015use –file externals%}.

Ultimately, the selection of a coolant depends on the reactor’s design philosophy and broader considerations such as cost, safety, and system efficiency. While there are many challenges, here we focus on one key design challenge associated with liquid metals.

How Magnetic Fields Reshape Liquid-Metal Cooling

The blanket operates within an intense magnetic field generated by the fusion plasma. As a result, the liquid metal flowing through it behaves as an electrically conducting fluid.

When a conducting fluid moves through a magnetic field, it experiences an opposing force known as the Lorentz force. This force resists the fluid’s motion, making the flow more laminar and reducing the coolant’s ability to carry away heat efficiently. The resulting decline in turbulence can threaten the thermal management of the reactor (see ).

To counter this effect, several design strategies have been proposed. One approach introduces obstacles within the flow channels to deliberately create turbulence in the liquid metal. The resulting increase in turbulent mixing enhances heat dissipation and helps restore cooling efficiency.

Since it is currently not possible to test these ideas through large-scale experiments, researchers rely on computer simulations. The study of how obstacles influence heat transfer in liquid-metal flows under strong magnetic fields forms a key part of magnetohydrodynamics (MHD).

Simulating this problem requires combining the Navier–Stokes equations that govern liquid-metal flow with the heat-transfer diffusion equations and the Maxwell equations that describe electromagnetic effects. Together, these form a coupled system of equations, making magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations both computationally demanding and numerically challenging. One of the key challenges in modeling turbulent flow is that small errors during computation, often caused by the limitations of the computer itself, can accumulate over time and lead to unrealistic results. Keeping such a complex system stable on a computer requires advanced computational algorithms that can control these growing errors while still preserving the essential physics of the problem.

Stable Simulation of Turbulent Magnetohydrodynamic Flow

To better understand how liquid metal behaves inside the magnetic field of a fusion reactor, I built a computer simulation framework that can model the flow, the magnetic forces, and the heat transfer all together. Instead of running experiments, which are nearly impossible under such extreme conditions, the simulation allows us to see how the coolant would move, how heat spreads, and where performance might fail.

At the heart of this work was designing a way to keep the simulation stable and realistic even when the flow becomes turbulent and the magnetic forces are strong. The model was tested under a range of flow and magnetic conditions to mimic what would happen inside an actual reactor blanket. The following are the key simulation insights from our work:

  • Stable modeling of liquid-metal flow: The simulation remained stable where standard models failed, capturing both turbulence and magnetic damping effects.

  • Heat-transfer behavior: Increasing magnetic field strength made the flow more laminar, reducing turbulence and heat-transfer efficiency.

  • Role of obstacles: Introducing obstacles reintroduced turbulence, enhancing heat removal.

  • Balance of forces: The Lorentz force counteracted motion, revealing the trade-off between stability and heat transport.

  • Validation of results: The model reproduced known physical trends and revealed insights inaccessible to direct experiments.

Flow 1
Flow 2

This study demonstrated that it is possible to numerically reproduce and analyze liquid-metal flow under strong magnetic confinement with reliable accuracy. Such models can guide the design of future fusion reactors by revealing how geometry, magnetic-field strength, and coolant properties together influence heat transfer and reactor safety.

item.title: Granular Mechanics with Graph Theory
item.description:
This article explores how tiny shifts between grains of sand or rock can lead to large-scale failures in tunnels and foundations. Existing experiments and simulations have shown how hidden networks of forces, called force chains, form and break within granular materials. Understanding these invisible structures helps engineers design safer and more resilient systems. We use graph theory to characterize force chains and then explore how particle size and variation in cohesion affect the assembly that leads to force chains.

When Solid Ground Turns Unpredictable

During the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake, the Longxi Road Tunnel, located near the epicenter, collapsed completely (see ). What seemed like stable rock suddenly crumbled into debris, burying the structure.

This failure illustrates that the surrounding rock mass did not behave as a rigid solid but as a granular material. Granular material is composed of countless small particles, such as sand, gravel, or grains of rice, that can behave like a solid in one moment and flow like a liquid in the next.

The disturbance during the earthquake caused the granular mass to transition from a solid-like to a fluid-like state. Similar disturbances can also occur during tunnel construction or operations.

The effect of such materials on tunnel stability is only one example of why understanding granular behavior is vital. Granular materials also play a pivotal role in the stability of other structures, such as bridges, buildings, and dams.

With rapid infrastructure development driven by economic growth, ensuring the safe construction and operation of engineering projects requires a deep understanding of how granular materials respond under different conditions.

But how can tiny movements between grains of sand or rock fragments cause an entire tunnel or slope to fail?

When Small Players (Particles) Change Everything

The answer lies in how the force from structures is shared among countless particles below. When these particles shift, even slightly, the balance that keeps the structure stable can change, creating weak zones that may suddenly give way.

Understanding this hidden interaction is key to explaining why granular materials sometimes behave unpredictably. This idea forms the basis for studying force chains, microscopic networks of particles that transfer forces much greater than those in their surroundings.

These force chains are often visualized in photoelastic experiments, as shown in . The video captures the motion of a circular object being pulled out from a bed of transparent, disk-shaped particles. As the object moves, bright patterns appear and disappear within the material. These bright patterns are the force chains, showing how contact forces build up, shift, and break during rapid motion.

Experimental observation of force chains

These chains function like a spinal cord, channeling forces through selective paths instead of spreading them evenly, silently deciding whether a structure remains stable or collapses. Understanding how these chains form and evolve helps explain the changes that occur in granular materials during the transition from a solid-like to a fluid-like state.

But what controls the formation and disappearance of these chains? Why do some granular materials develop strong, continuous force networks, while others remain fragmented or lose them entirely? To answer these questions, we turn to our computational study, which explores how particle size, packing, and cohesion shape the emergence of force chains in granular systems.

From Particle Properties to Assembly: The Birth of Force Chains

To explore what shapes these hidden networks inside granular materials, we built a digital model that simulates how thousands of tiny particles press, move, and settle under pressure. In this virtual setup, we changed two factors, particle size and particle attraction, resulting in a change in packing density. This helped us see how these factors influence the invisible patterns of force inside the material.

The results were revealing. Even a slight difference in particle size created visible force paths within the material. But when the difference became too large, the system lost its structure. The once organized network of forces broke apart, making the material weaker and more unpredictable.

The two videos below show this difference. On the right is a neatly packed system in which forces flow smoothly through regular patterns. On the left is an unevenly packed system where the same load spreads unevenly through scattered paths. The bright areas show the particles carrying more force. Together, they illustrate how slight variations in particle arrangement can completely alter materials’ behavior.

Force chains in an irregular system **(Left)** and absence of force chains in a well-arranged system under compression **(Right)**. Refer {%cite 10.1115/1.4068059 --file papers %}

When the attraction between particles increased, the number of strong force paths decreased. The forces became more evenly shared among many particles, creating a smoother but less concentrated pattern. In simple terms, a stronger attraction between particles made the material more uniform, but also less able to carry large forces along distinct paths.

These results show that the way tiny particles arrange and interact can decide whether a structure remains stable or fails. Understanding these hidden force networks helps engineers design stronger and safer materials and foundations.
